content: Imagine waking up one day, and all the vehicles in the world - cars, buses, airplanes - just stopped working. The roads are silent, the petrol pumps are closed, and nobody can travel far. Why did this happen? What magical liquid disappeared from the Earth?
Can you guess what this 'magical liquid' is? Why do vehicles need it to move? What would happen if we used it all up?

content.title: The Journey of Petroleum
content.description: Petroleum is formed from the remains of ancient sea plants and animals over millions of years. It's like nature's very slow pressure cooker!

content: Think of a car as a human body. Just like we need food for energy to run and play, vehicles need fuel (like petrol or diesel) for energy to move. This fuel comes from deep inside the Earth.

The 'magical liquid' is **Petroleum**. It is a dark, thick, smelly liquid found deep under the Earth. We get petrol, diesel, kerosene, and even LPG (cooking gas) from it. It takes millions of years to form, so it is a limited resource.

concept: A naturally occurring liquid found beneath the Earth's surface that can be refined into fuel.

question: What happens if a vehicle does not get any fuel like petrol or diesel?

content: Take a moment to think: How many vehicles do you see on the road every day? If petroleum takes millions of years to form, are we using it faster than nature can make it?
Many people think that petrol is made quickly in factories. In reality, it takes millions of years to form naturally under the Earth, which is why it can finish if we use it too fast!
Not just vehicles, fuel is also used for cooking (LPG), making plastics, and running big machines in factories. If petroleum finishes, it affects almost everything in our daily life!

Be an Energy Detective! Count how many vehicles your family uses. Discuss with your parents how you can save fuel (like carpooling, using a bicycle, or turning off the engine at a red light). Write down three ways you can help save petroleum.
Have you ever noticed people turning off their vehicle's engine while waiting at a red traffic signal? Why do you think they do that instead of just waiting?
Every second an engine is on, it drinks fuel. If you wait for 2 minutes at a red light with the engine running, are you wasting fuel for no reason?

content.title: Droplets of Fuel
content.description: Imagine a leaking tap wasting water drop by drop. An idling engine wastes fuel drop by drop in the exact same way!

content: **Conservation** of fuel means using it carefully so it lasts longer. Turning off the engine at a red light, using public transport like buses, or walking for short distances are smart ways to conserve our limited fuel.

concept: The careful use and protection of resources to prevent them from finishing.

question: Which of the following is a good habit to save fuel?
options: Keeping the engine on at a red light
Using a bicycle for short distances

content: What if everyone in your city decided to use public transport like buses and trains for one day? How much fuel would be saved?
Ask students to calculate how much money their family could save in a month if they reduced their fuel usage by just 10%.
Saving fuel doesn't just save money and resources; it also keeps the air cleaner! Less fuel burned means less smoke and pollution, leading to healthier breathing for everyone.
Design a poster for your school to encourage teachers and parents to switch off their vehicle engines at traffic lights to save fuel and reduce pollution!
